{{Short description|American planetary scientist (1939–2026)}}
'''Laurence E. Nyquist''' (July 28, 1939 – August 5, 2026) was an American [[planetary science|planetary scientist]] for the [[National Aeronautics and Space Administration]]. He was known for his contributions to knowledge of the [[chronometry]] of planetary materials, which have been important in understanding time-scales for accretion, differentiation, and impacts on [[meteorite]] parent bodies.<ref>Schmadel, Lutz D. "Dictionary of Minor Planet Names". Springer Science & Business Media, 2012, p. 524.</ref> His NASA biography also records contributions to the study of [[noble gases]] in iron meteorites and lunar samples, [[radiometric age dating]] and [[isotope geochemistry]] of lunar, Martian, and meteoric samples, and the application of stable isotope methods to [[biomedical research]]. He served as an associate editor of ''[[Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta]]'' and [[Lunar and Planetary Science Conference|''Proceedings of the Lunar and Planetary Science Conference'']].

Nyquist received a [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] in physics and mathematics from [[Macalester College]] in 1961, an [[M.S.]] and [[Ph.D.]], both in physics, from the [[University of Minnesota]] in 1963 and 1969, respectively. [[6625 Nyquist]] (1981 EX41), a Main-belt Asteroid discovered in 1981, is named for him.

Nyquist died on August 5, 2026, at the age of 87.<ref>[https://www.dignitymemorial.com/obituaries/webster-tx/laurence-nyquist-12994273 Laurence Elwood Nyquist]</ref>
